executive_summary: AUD/JPY closed at 110.81356 on 30 October 2026, which means 1 Australian dollar bought 110.81 yen. A rising pair is a stronger Australian dollar. The cross is +1.13% over one month, -0.30% over three months, -2.02% over six months and +9.45% over one year, and it sits at the 74th percentile of its 52-week closing range (99.289-114.83705). The main story for the pair is the timing of the two central banks. The RBA decides on 3 November, where a hike to 4.85% is 80-88% priced and would widen the policy gap from 335bp to 360bp. The Bank of Japan does not decide until 18 December, where a hike to 1.50% is about 75% priced. Positioning is crowded against the pair on both legs at once: speculators hold a 128,300-contract net short in Australian dollar futures and a 101,600-contract net long in yen futures. The two horizons point in opposite directions. The tactical stance is Bullish, conviction 2 (score +0.1153), based on peak carry and covering of those crowded shorts. The strategic stance is Bearish, conviction 2 (score -0.2286), because the RBA is likely to stop at 4.85% while the Bank of Japan keeps hiking. Our base cases are 112.20 over the next four weeks and 107.00 by late April 2027. The second figure is 181 pips below the six-month forward of 108.81 and roughly 325 pips below the aggregated bank path. The tactical call is the more fragile of the two. It clears the Bullish threshold by only 0.0153, and spot sits 46-117 pips below a 50-, 100- and 200-day moving-average band at 111.27-111.99. We therefore run it as a small, tightly stopped carry trade that we expect to close out into that band, not as a position to hold.

market_context.valuation_assessment: Valuation is stretched in the Australian dollar's favour by every long-run measure. World Bank PPP conversion factors put fair AUD/JPY near 69.40, so spot is about 60% above that level. The BIS real effective exchange rate is 116.13 for Australia (the highest in G10+SGD) against 66.61 for Japan (the lowest by 26.8 points). That is the widest real-exchange-rate gap of any G10 pair. What the level prices is carry, not mean reversion: a 335bp policy gap and a deeply negative Japanese real policy rate (about -0.85) against a positive Australian one. Valuation of this size does not drive the cross inside six months on its own. It matters as an asymmetry: if carry stops paying, there is a long way down to anything resembling fair value.

market_context.recent_regime: AUD/JPY is a carry cross caught between its widest policy gap of the cycle and a run of shocks that hit it from the yen side. Each of the three summer peaks near 114.5-115.0 was ended by an external event: the late-July intervention, a sharp early-September drop from 113.81 to 112.19, and the RBA repricing that bottomed with a 109.32 close on 30 September. October was a recovery driven by RBA repricing, from 109.57 to an intraday high of 111.56 on 29 October. It survived the 15 October iron-ore two-year low (intraday 108.66) and the 22 October semiconductor sell-off (a 113-pip fall to 110.11). The Bank of Japan's hawkish hold on 30 October took the cross back to 110.81 with an intraday low of 110.21. Analysts flag the same tension for the week ahead: yen-buying intervention could strengthen Japan's currency and push AUD/JPY lower, against an RBA decision on Tuesday, November 3, at 2:30 p.m. The cross climbed about 15.7% from its year-ago trough, then spent May-October capped near 114.5-115.0 while its lows stepped lower.

Carry regime: favourable for now. It is the widest yen carry in G10 alongside NOK, with vol at 7.3-8.2% in contango, but it is vulnerable to the risk-off channel (Factor 3) and to the gap narrowing over the strategic horizon. tactical.bilateral_analysis: The policy gap is 335bp: an RBA cash rate target of 4.60% (as of 29 October) against a Bank of Japan call rate of 1.25% (as of 27 October). The only scheduled decision in the four-week window is the RBA on 3 November. The Bank of Japan does not meet until 18 December, so nothing on the calendar can narrow the gap before the window closes. ASX cash-rate futures put the odds of a hike to 4.85% at about 80% on 29 October, and reports after the 28 October CPI put them at 85-88%. That means roughly 20-22bp of the 25bp is already priced, and a hike would take the gap to 360bp. The annualised roll between the November and December crosses implied by CME Australian dollar and yen futures was 361.3bp on 29 October, almost exactly the gap after a hike. Forwards therefore already carry the move, although that measure also contains cross-currency basis. The edge relative to pricing is small. The bullish case rests on the gap being at its widest with no Japanese meeting to compress it, and on carry of roughly 31-33 pips a month on a carry-to-implied-vol ratio near 0.43-0.46. The asymmetric risk is a hold, which would take about 20bp out of the Australian front end at once. A hike framed as the last one would widen the gap but flatten the expected path.

tactical.what_is_priced: Most of the 3 November hike is priced, both in cash-rate futures and in the futures roll, which already sits at the post-hike differential. What is not priced is how long the gap stays at its widest: no Japanese decision falls before 18 December, so the four-week window earns peak carry. A hold is the unpriced tail, at 12-20%.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the gap's direction matters more than its level, and the direction is narrowing. If the RBA hikes to 4.85% on 3 November, the meeting list then has the RBA on 8 December, where a hold is priced, and on 9 February. The Bank of Japan meets on 18 December, where a hike to 1.50% is about 75% priced, and on 22 January with an Outlook Report, the natural point to guide or deliver the next step. On that path the gap goes from 360bp to 335bp by year-end, and to 310bp if the Bank of Japan moves again in the window. Swaps price nearly 75bp of Japanese tightening over twelve months, so the yen leg is largely in the price. The edge sits on the Australian leg. Cash-rate futures still price a second RBA hike by around mid-2027, while employment fell 39,300 in September and unemployment rose for three straight months to 4.7%. That points to a 4.85% peak and a 10-15bp dovish gap against pricing. The 10-year spread of 236.7bp at end-October also reflects a 26bp fall in Australian 10-year yields in October. The level of carry stays large and supportive, which is why confidence is only just above even. But the expectations channel turns against the pair once the RBA stops and the Bank of Japan keeps going.

factors.horizon_split: Tactically the only decision in the window is the RBA's, which can only widen the gap, and no Japanese meeting falls before 18 December, so carry is at its peak. Strategically the 18 December and 22 January Bank of Japan meetings and a likely Australian peak make the gap narrow, and the dovish gap to pricing sits on the Australian side. The stance therefore flips from a low-confidence Bullish to a low-confidence Bearish.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: On levels the inflation gap is wide and growth favours Australia. Australian monthly CPI was 4.3% in September and the September-quarter trimmed mean 3.7%. Japanese CPI excluding fresh food was 2.1%, the measure that also excludes energy 2.4%, and Tokyo's October core 2.6%. Australian GDP is up 2.1% y/y against 0.7% for Japan. Momentum points the other way. Australian employment fell 39,300 in September, unemployment rose to 4.7% and the October composite PMI dropped to 47.7. In Japan inflation is broadening, with cash earnings up 3.8% y/y and the Bank of Japan's trimmed-mean core at 2.5%. Real policy rates are about +0.3 to +0.9 in Australia against roughly -0.85 in Japan, so the real gap still favours AUD but is shrinking from both sides. The window holds offsetting releases: Japan's Q3 GDP on 16 November, where the consensus is about +0.08% annualised and a negative print would weigh on December hike odds; Japanese national CPI on 20 November; Australian wages on 18 November; the Australian labour force in the third week of November; and Australian monthly CPI on 25 November. A soft Japanese GDP print helps the pair and a weak Australian jobs print hurts it, and both are plausible in the same fortnight. The factor is Neutral.

tactical.what_is_priced: Australian pricing reflects the CPI surprise but not the labour-market slide. Japanese pricing reflects firm inflation and wages but largely ignores a possible Q3 contraction. Each side carries an unpriced downside surprise of similar size inside the window, so neither direction has an edge.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the two economies are at different points in the cycle, and the gap favours the yen. Australian inflation is cost-push: fuel rose 9.4% in September alone, electricity is up 12.8%, goods inflation is 4.6% against services at 4.1%, and wages are growing 3.2% against 4.3% inflation. That mix, in an economy where unemployment has risen from 4.5% to 4.7% in three months, usually ends with the central bank stopping early. Japan's inflation is becoming self-sustaining. The Tankan puts firms' price expectations at 2.5-2.6% at one to five years, the 2026 Shunto settled at 5.01%, and the Bank of Japan raised its FY2027 core CPI forecast to 2.6% in the 30 October Outlook Report. The AUD dossier expects Q3 GDP on 2 December at 0.2-0.3% q/q and unemployment near 4.9% by February. The JPY dossier treats Japan's growth as weak but not recessionary, with capex plans up 7.6%. Relative data momentum therefore supports continued Japanese normalisation and an end to Australian tightening, which works on the pair through the rate path. The upside risk is an Australian expectations spiral, with Melbourne Institute expectations at 5.3%, but falling real wages make it unlikely within the window.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: This is a pure risk-proxy cross: the Australian dollar has the highest equity and China beta in G10, and the yen is the main funding currency of the carry trade. Risk signals are deteriorating under a calm surface. The VIX was 17.2 on 29 October, mid-range. US high-yield spreads, however, widened 18bp in a month to 326bp, the 95th percentile of their one-year range, with investment grade at 89bp, the 96th percentile. The Nikkei lost 8.22% in October to about 63,290 and the Philadelphia semiconductor index fell 6.7% on 22 October on AI-spending doubts. China's October manufacturing PMI fell to 49.3, which hits the Australian leg directly. Both dossiers read the same tape the same way for this cross: the AUD view is Bearish on risk and the JPY view is Bullish on risk. The two signals reinforce rather than cancel. The transmission is a carry unwind, as in July-August 2024 when the VIX jumped from about 16 to 38 in four sessions and yen funding positions were cut. The JPY dossier puts the chance of a VIX move above 25 within four weeks at about 25%. The caveat is the energy channel: a Gulf escalation that lifts oil hurts the yen through its import bill, which can blunt the yen's haven response.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the risk channel is two-sided for this cross because the main global shock is an energy war rather than a financial crisis. In risk-off driven by credit or AI capex, the cross falls through carry unwinds, Australian super-fund hedge rebalancing and Japanese repatriation. In risk-off driven by oil, the yen's terms-of-trade loss competes with its haven role: during the summer escalation the yen weakened against the dollar until the Ministry of Finance intervened. A Gulf settlement would be risk-on, which helps AUD, but it would also lower oil and LNG, which helps the yen. China's Q3 GDP beat at 4.5% y/y, and the December Central Economic Work Conference is an upside risk for the Australian leg, while the 49.3 PMI is a downside one. The AUD dossier puts a risk-off episode and a risk-on extension at about 25% each over six months, and the JPY dossier scores the factor Neutral strategically. With balanced tails and a central case of range trading, the factor has no directional signal. High-yield spreads above 400bp would turn it Bearish, and a return below 280bp would turn it Bullish.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The CFTC data for the week to 27 October make the pair-implied position unusually one-sided because the two legs reinforce each other. In Australian dollar futures, asset managers are net short 125,237 contracts and the legacy non-commercial net short is 128,300, beyond the -80,000 level that has historically marked AUD extremes. In yen futures, asset managers are net long 91,191 contracts, the high of the 25 weeks since May, and the legacy net long is 101,600, beyond the +80,000 stretch level. Specs are short the base and long the quote at once, which amounts to a crowded short in AUD/JPY. Both dossiers read this as contrarian support for the pair: Bullish on the AUD leg, and Bearish on the yen leg because a stretched long is at risk of liquidation. The yen long was built in a month with no Japanese decision and runs into a window with none either. The Australian short faces a likely hike on 3 November. The unwind triggers are therefore dated: a hawkish RBA on 3 November, Governor Ueda's remarks on 6 November or a Summary of Opinions that leaves December open, and a weak Japanese Q3 GDP print on 16 November. Option skew points the same way on the yen leg, where hedgers pay for a weaker yen, but the other way on the AUD leg, where puts are bid.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the crowded pair short works as a cushion more than a driver. The Australian short was built on terms of trade, with iron ore near USD 90 and a record current-account deficit. The AUD dossier notes that shorts like this were held for two to three quarters in 2015 and 2019 before covering. The yen long reads as a structural reallocation that built over two Bank of Japan hikes, so it need not unwind quickly either. Two slow flows matter for this cross specifically. The first is Japanese real-money demand for Australian bonds, which pay a 236.7bp 10-year pickup over JGBs. That pickup is larger than the hedged pickup available on US Treasuries, which supports AUD against JPY even as Japanese investors repatriate from the dollar. The second is Japanese fiscal year-end repatriation in late February and March, which supports the yen at the edge of the window. On balance the marginal seller of the cross is scarce: specs are already short AUD and long JPY, so further pair downside needs new sellers. That caps the downside more than it creates upside. The stance flips to Neutral if the Australian asset-manager short covers above -60,000 contracts or the yen legacy long falls back toward +50,000 without a fundamental trigger.

net_commodity_exposure.net_effect_calculation: Step 1, LNG: JKM up is strongly negative for JPY and sometimes positive for AUD as an LNG exporter, so the pair rises. Step 3, iron ore: down is negative for AUD and mildly positive for Japan as a steel-making importer, so the pair falls. Step 4, netting: energy is up sharply (JKM +27% m/m, Brent around USD 110-114) while iron ore is down near a two-year low. In the near term the energy steps outweigh iron ore because Japan's energy deficit is widening monthly and Japanese purchases of Australian energy transfer income bilaterally, so the net effect is modestly bullish for the pair. Over quarters the iron ore loss accumulates in Australia's national income and current account and brings the net back toward neutral.

The crowded two-leg pair short limits how far the cross can fall without new sellers. Japan's fiscal expansion, quantified in the late-December budget, has weakened rather than strengthened the yen in this cycle. What is priced is a gradually narrowing gap with Australian rates still on hold-to-higher. What we expect is narrowing from both ends, with the Australian side surprising dovishly. cross_horizon_consistency.explanation: The horizons diverge because the calendar does. Inside four weeks the only scheduled decision is the RBA's on 3 November, which can only widen the 335bp gap, and positioning is crowded against the pair with dated catalysts for covering on both legs. Over one to three months the 18 December and 22 January Bank of Japan decisions narrow the gap, Australian labour data push the RBA toward a peak, and the weights shift toward the policy-guidance block. The Policy and Guidance factors flip from positive or zero to negative.
cross_horizon_consistency.inflection_point: The December cluster: RBA on 8 December, where a hold is priced, FOMC on 9 December and the Bank of Japan on 18 December, where a hike to 1.50% is about 75% priced. The 22 January Outlook Report meeting and the 9 February RBA decision confirm or reverse the turn. Earlier signals would be a weak Australian October labour force in the third week of November and firm Japanese CPI on 20 November.
cross_horizon_consistency.trading_implication: Treat the tactical upside as a carry-and-squeeze window to be harvested rather than held. Build strategic bearish exposure as the December cluster approaches, preferably through optionality rather than outright forward sales, which pay about 360bp a year. In levels: the two trade plans share one hand-off zone, 111.90-112.40, where the tactical long takes profit and the strategic short starts building, at the 100-/200-day band. If the tactical long never reaches that zone and is stopped below 109.50, the strategic short is still valid; in that case, enter through puts rather than spot, because a sold-off cross has already used up part of the base-case move.

assumptions: Price series: daily open, high, low and close for AUD/JPY, 130 weekday sessions from 2026-05-04 to 2026-10-30. Spot is 110.81356 at the 30 October close. The valuation date of 1 November is a Sunday, so the two-day gap is a weekend with no missed sessions. Every level, pip distance, percentage and forward is anchored to that close. Web quotes near 110.82-110.90 on 2 November were not used. Pip size is 0.01.

Moving averages are simple averages of trading-day closes. They and the support/resistance zones are computed over the full stored history of 4,919 weekday sessions from 2007-12-24 to 2026-10-30, recorded as 1,010 weekly and 502 monthly bars. The 130 daily sessions are the window for the price-action narrative. Zone distances are quoted to zone midpoints unless an edge is specified.

Zone shortfall: only one resistance zone and nine support zones met the two-touch threshold. The resistance side is supplemented with round numbers (112.00, 115.00) and the moving-average band, labelled as a lower class of evidence than the computed zones.
Realised volatility is annualised on 252 trading days. ATR(14) is 0.90495 (90 pips).

Rates: policy rates are the RBA cash rate target of 4.60% as of 29 October and the Bank of Japan call rate of 1.25% as of 27 October, a 335bp gap. The 10-year yields alongside the price series are monthly readings as of 1 September (Australia 5.283%, Japan 3.05%, spread 223.3bp) and are not quoted as live. Live comparisons use the 30 October closes of 5.137% and 2.770% (236.7bp).

Implied volatility: cross implied volatility (7.284%, 7.754% and 8.227% at 35.7, 98.7 and 189.6 days, observed 29 October) is an estimate built from CME options on each leg and a realised correlation of 0.4612. This method has understated quoted cross vol by 9-18%, so it is treated as a floor. No cross implied-vol percentile or risk reversal exists (iv_percentile is therefore null).

Forwards: forward points come from the -361.3bp annualised CME futures roll (29 October), which combines the interest differential and basis, applied linearly to spot. Annualised carry for a long is signed positive at +335bp (policy differential); the roll premium is the forward discount of AUD.

Positioning: CFTC positioning is for the AUD and JPY futures legs against the dollar, week to 27 October. The pair-implied position is inferred by combining the legs. The report states a 96th-percentile figure for the yen leg only; no AUD-leg percentile is stated, so it is null.
Bilateral trade: IMF Direction of Trade Statistics for 2024: Australian exports to Japan US$46.7bn, imports US$17.7bn, net US$29.0bn; Japanese imports from Australia US$52.9bn.

How stances and levels were set: the factor stances were scored on rates, macro data, policy communications, positioning, trade and cross-asset evidence, without reference to the pair's own recent trading. The chart is used only for levels, entries, stops, targets, sizing and the Factor 9 context.

Scenario targets: the strategic base case of 107.00 cross-checks against the two currency dossiers' six-month paths (0.6950 × 154.00 = 107.03). The downside target of 102.50 is the 200-week average projected forward at its current slope of about 0.1025 a week.
Consensus sources: the bank consensus comes from secondary aggregations of bank research. Model-driven forecast sites found during research were excluded.
Dossier dates are not stated in the report; metadata dates use the report's analysis date of 2026-11-01.
